notes.definition: Blood is a tissue consisting of plasma, in which red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended. Each component has a specific function in transport, defence or clotting.
explanation: Blood is a tissue because it contains cells working together for a shared function. About 55% of blood is plasma, a pale straw-coloured liquid. The rest is mostly red blood cells, with a very small proportion of white blood cells and platelets. If blood is spun in a centrifuge, these separate into layers.

Plasma transports dissolved substances around the body. These include carbon dioxide from the organs to the lungs, soluble products of digestion (such as glucose and amino acids) from the small intestine to other organs, urea from the liver to the kidneys, hormones, and proteins such as antibodies. Plasma also distributes heat around the body.

Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to body cells. They contain the red pigment haemoglobin, which combines with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases it in the tissues. They are adapted in three main ways: they have no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin; they are biconcave discs, giving a large surface area to volume ratio for oxygen to diffuse in and out; and they are small and flexible, so they can squeeze through narrow capillaries.

White blood cells are part of the immune system and defend the body against pathogens. Unlike red blood cells, they have a nucleus. Some (phagocytes) engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis; some have a lobed nucleus that helps them squeeze out of capillaries into tissues. Others (lymphocytes) have a large nucleus and produce antibodies and antitoxins. You will meet these in more detail in the topic on infection and response.

Platelets are small fragments of cells with no nucleus. At a wound they help the blood to clot, forming a scab. This stops excessive blood loss and prevents pathogens entering the body. In exams you may be shown a photograph or drawing of blood cells and asked to identify them: red cells are the most numerous and have no nucleus, white cells are larger with a nucleus, and platelets are tiny fragments.
keyFacts: Blood is a tissue made of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Plasma is about 55% of blood volume.
Plasma carries carbon dioxide, glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and antibodies, and transfers heat.
Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.
Red blood cells have no nucleus and a biconcave shape (large surface area to volume ratio).
White blood cells have a nucleus and defend against pathogens (phagocytosis, antibodies, antitoxins).
Platelets are cell fragments that help blood clot.
Red blood cells are the most numerous cells in blood; a human red blood cell is about 7 to 8 μm across.

keyTerms.definition: The straw-coloured liquid part of blood, which transports dissolved substances, cells and heat.
A biconcave cell with no nucleus that carries oxygen using haemoglobin.
The red protein in red blood cells that combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin.
A blood cell with a nucleus that helps defend the body against pathogens.
A small fragment of a cell, with no nucleus, that helps blood to clot.
The process by which a white blood cell engulfs and digests a pathogen.
Curved inwards on both sides, like a disc pressed in at the centre.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plasma carries oxygen.
misconceptions.right: In fact almost all oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells. Plasma carries carbon dioxide, food molecules, urea, hormones and antibodies.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think platelets are whole cells.
misconceptions.right: In fact platelets are small fragments of cells and have no nucleus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think red blood cells have a nucleus like most cells.
misconceptions.right: In fact mature human red blood cells have no nucleus, which leaves more space for haemoglobin.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think blood is not a tissue because it is a liquid.
misconceptions.right: In fact blood is a tissue: it is made of cells (and plasma) working together to carry out transport and defence.

realWorld: Blood donations are separated into red cells, plasma and platelets so each can be given to the patients who need it.
People with anaemia have too little haemoglobin or too few red blood cells, so they feel tired and breathless.
A blood count measures the numbers of red cells, white cells and platelets; a high white cell count can indicate an infection.
examTips: Learn the four components and one function for each; this is a very common 4-mark question.
When explaining red blood cell adaptations, link each feature to its function (for example 'no nucleus, so more room for haemoglobin, so more oxygen carried').
To identify cells in a micrograph, use number and nucleus: many cells with no nucleus are red cells, a few larger cells with a nucleus are white cells.
Give named examples of what plasma carries and where from and to, for example 'urea from the liver to the kidneys'.
summary: Blood is a tissue: plasma plus red cells, white cells and platelets.
Plasma transports dissolved substances and heat.
Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; biconcave, no nucleus.
White blood cells defend against pathogens; they have a nucleus.
Platelets are cell fragments that help blood clot.

flashcards.front: Name the four components of blood.
flashcards.back: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets.

flashcards.front: What percentage of blood is plasma?
Name four substances carried in plasma.
flashcards.back: Carbon dioxide, glucose (or amino acids), urea, hormones (also antibodies).

flashcards.front: Where does plasma carry urea from and to?
flashcards.back: From the liver to the kidneys.

flashcards.front: What is the function of red blood cells?
flashcards.back: To carry oxygen from the lungs to body cells.
Combines with oxygen in the lungs (oxyhaemoglobin) and releases it in tissues.

flashcards.front: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?
flashcards.back: More room for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried.

flashcards.front: Why are red blood cells biconcave?
flashcards.back: Large surface area to volume ratio for fast diffusion of oxygen.

flashcards.front: What is the function of white blood cells?
flashcards.back: Defend the body against pathogens (phagocytosis, antibodies, antitoxins).

flashcards.front: How can you recognise a white blood cell in a micrograph?
flashcards.back: Larger than a red blood cell and has a nucleus; far fewer of them.
Small fragments of cells with no nucleus that help blood clot.
Stops blood loss and prevents pathogens entering through wounds.

questions.question: Which component of blood carries oxygen?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen.

questions.question: What is the function of platelets?
questions.explanation: Platelets are cell fragments that help form clots at wounds.

questions.question: Which component makes up about 55% of the volume of blood?
questions.explanation: Plasma is just over half the volume. Red blood cells are about 45%; white cells and platelets are under 1%.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT carried dissolved in plasma?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is inside red blood cells. Urea, glucose and carbon dioxide are dissolved in plasma.

questions.question: Which feature allows a red blood cell to carry more oxygen?
options: It has no nucleus, so there is more room for haemoglobin
questions.explanation: Without a nucleus there is extra space for haemoglobin. Engulfing pathogens is a white blood cell function.

questions.question: A student sees a large cell with a lobed nucleus in a blood smear. What is it?
questions.explanation: Only white blood cells have a nucleus in blood. Red blood cells and platelets have none.

questions.question: Plasma carries urea from:
options: the small intestine to the liver
questions.explanation: Urea is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys.

questions.question: Why is the biconcave shape of red blood cells an advantage?
options: It gives a large surface area to volume ratio for oxygen to diffuse in and out quickly
It allows the cell to divide quickly
It makes room for a nucleus
It helps the cell engulf pathogens
questions.explanation: The dimpled disc shape increases surface area relative to volume, speeding up diffusion of oxygen.

questions.question: A person has a low platelet count. Which symptom is most likely?
options: Bruising easily and bleeding for longer from cuts
High levels of urea in the blood
questions.explanation: Platelets help blood clot, so too few means poor clotting. Breathlessness suggests too few red cells; frequent infections suggest too few white cells.

questions.question: At high altitude there is less oxygen in the air. After several weeks there, a climber's blood would be expected to contain:
questions.explanation: More red blood cells (and haemoglobin) compensate for the lower oxygen concentration, so more oxygen can be transported.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares red and white blood cells?
options: Both contain haemoglobin, but only white cells have a nucleus
Red cells are more numerous and have no nucleus; white cells are fewer and have a nucleus
White cells are more numerous and smaller than red cells
Red cells defend against pathogens; white cells carry oxygen
questions.explanation: There are hundreds of red cells for every white cell. White cells have a nucleus and no haemoglobin.

questions.question: An adult has 5.0 dm³ of blood. 55% of this is plasma. Calculate the volume of plasma.
A red blood cell has a real diameter of 8 μm. In a drawing it is 24 mm across. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
questions.explanation: Convert the image size to μm: 24 × 1000 = 24 000 μm. Magnification = 24 000 ÷ 8 = × 3000.

questions.question: A micrograph is magnified × 1500. A white blood cell in the image is 18 mm across. Calculate the real diameter of the cell in μm.
questions.explanation: Real size = image ÷ magnification = 18 ÷ 1500 = 0.012 mm = 12 μm. This is larger than a red blood cell (about 7 to 8 μm), as expected.

questions.question: 1 mm³ of blood contains 5 000 000 red blood cells and 8000 white blood cells. Calculate how many red blood cells there are for every white blood cell.
A healthy platelet count is 250 000 per mm³. A patient's count is 90 000 per mm³. Calculate the percentage decrease compared with the healthy value.
Name the red pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.question: Give two substances transported by plasma.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: carbon dioxide; glucose / amino acids / soluble products of digestion; urea; hormones; antibodies / proteins
questions.explanation: Plasma transports many dissolved substances. Oxygen is not a correct answer as it is carried by red blood cells.

questions.question: Explain three ways a red blood cell is adapted to carry oxygen.
markScheme: 1 mark: no nucleus so more room for haemoglobin
1 mark: biconcave shape gives a large surface area to volume ratio for diffusion
1 mark: small and flexible so can pass through narrow capillaries
questions.explanation: Each adaptation must be linked to the reason it helps.

questions.question: Explain why blood clotting at a cut is important.
markScheme: 1 mark: prevents pathogens / microorganisms entering the body
questions.explanation: A clot seals the wound, reducing blood loss and acting as a barrier to infection.

questions.question: Explain why blood is described as a tissue.
markScheme: 1 mark: it consists of cells (red, white, platelets) with plasma
1 mark: working together to carry out a function such as transport / defence
questions.explanation: A tissue is a group of cells working together for a shared function, which describes blood.

questions.question: A blood smear shows many small cells without a nucleus, a few larger cells with a nucleus, and tiny fragments. Identify each type and suggest why the white blood cells are much less numerous than red blood cells.
acceptedAnswers: only needed in large numbers during infection
markScheme: 1 mark: small cells without nucleus are red blood cells; larger cells with nucleus are white blood cells
1 mark: red cells must carry oxygen to all cells all the time, while white cells are only needed in large numbers when pathogens are present / numbers increase during infection
questions.explanation: Identification uses size, nucleus and number. The difference in numbers reflects continuous oxygen demand compared with defence needed mainly during infection.

questions.question: A person has a disorder in which their red blood cells contain less haemoglobin than normal. Suggest why this person feels tired during exercise.
markScheme: 1 mark: less oxygen is carried to muscle cells
1 mark: so less aerobic respiration / less energy transferred, or more anaerobic respiration producing lactic acid
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin carries oxygen. Less oxygen delivered means less aerobic respiration in muscles.

questions.question: State the function of white blood cells.
markScheme: 1 mark: to defend the body against pathogens / infection
questions.explanation: White blood cells are part of the immune system.

questions.question: Describe the functions of the four main components of blood.
markScheme: Indicative content: plasma: liquid that transports dissolved substances such as carbon dioxide to the lungs, glucose and amino acids from the small intestine, urea from liver to kidneys, hormones, antibodies, and heat; red blood cells: carry oxygen from the lungs to the body using haemoglobin; white blood cells: defend against pathogens by phagocytosis and producing antibodies and antitoxins; platelets: help blood clot at wounds to stop bleeding and prevent entry of pathogens.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a correct function for all four components, with detail such as named substances or how defence or clotting works.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): functions given for one or two components, or vague descriptions.
questions.explanation: Name all four components and give a clear function for each; extra detail moves an answer to the top level.

questions.question: Compare the structure of red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, and explain how the structure of each is related to its function.
markScheme: Indicative content: red blood cells: biconcave disc, no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin, small and flexible; function: carry oxygen; no nucleus leaves room for more haemoglobin; biconcave shape gives large surface area to volume ratio for diffusion; flexible to pass through capillaries. White blood cells: larger, have a nucleus (sometimes lobed), no haemoglobin; function: defence; phagocytes can change shape to engulf pathogens and squeeze out of capillaries; lymphocytes have a large nucleus containing the genes to make antibodies and antitoxins. Platelets: small fragments of cells, no nucleus; function: clotting at wounds; their small size means many can gather at a wound. Comparison points: number (red far more numerous), size (white largest, platelets smallest), presence of nucleus (only white cells).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison across all three with clear structure-to-function links.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): structure and function described for at least two, with some comparison.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or two components.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs direct statements such as 'unlike red blood cells, white blood cells have a nucleus', not separate descriptions.

questions.question: Which part of blood is a straw-coloured liquid?
questions.explanation: Plasma is the pale yellow liquid in which the cells are suspended.
